body_markdown:
IT administrators often automate repetitive lifecycle-management tasks to improve consistency and reduce manual effort. This takes work, and the ability to automate products via scripts, automations or APIs can become a critical requirement.


In today’s article, we’ll look at how Nutanix Lifecycle Manager (LCM) bundle management can be automated. Whilst this would be common in dark site or isolated environments, these approaches can be applied to connected environments, too.


## What are LCM bundles?


In LCM terminology, a “bundle” is a distributed package made available by Nutanix and Nutanix integration partners. Depending on the bundle type, an LCM bundle can include metadata such as version information, prerequisites, and files used by an LCM-managed component.


LCM bundles are distributed via the[Nutanix Support Portal](https://portal.nutanix.com/) . For the purposes of this article, we’ll work with a small bundle called the Security Databoard CVE Data, a package containing[CVE](https://www.cve.org/) (Critical Vulnerabilities and Exploits) info for the Prism Central Security Dashboard. This bundle was chosen for its size; only around 29KB for the current version, making it perfect for a demo.


**Important note** : Many Nutanix LCM bundles exceed the AWS CLI 5GB single-part upload limit. Whilst this article focuses on a single-part upload, Nutanix Objects Lite supports large, multi-part uploads when using` create-multipart-upload` and associated parameters. For more details on multi-part uploads, see[Uploading Files to Objects Lite Using AWS CLI – Multipart Upload](https://portal.nutanix.com/page/documents/details?targetId=Prism-Central-Guide-vpc_2024_3_1:mul-uploading-to-objects-lite-using-aws-cli-multipart-pc-t.html) .


LCM bundles are available for a range of Nutanix components. Available bundles depend on the environment and the downloads exposed through the Nutanix Support Portal. Examples of core components include Prism Central, AOS and AHV whilst examples of optional components include Nutanix Files Storage, Nutanix Objects Storage and NCM Self-Service. Existing customers can view available downloads on the[Nutanix Support Portal downloads page](https://portal.nutanix.com/page/downloads/list) .


## Demo Environment


The demo environment used throughout today’s demo is as follows:


- AOS 7.6.0.8 (at the time of writing this article, the latest AOS version is 7.6.0.11)
- Prism Central 7.6.0.10 (latest at the time of writing this article)
- AHV 11.0.0.2 (at the time of writing, the latest AHV version is 11.2.0.6)
- AWS CLI 2.31.33
- Prism Central cluster extId 8f5d9aaf-9ef7-405e-93ff-77385d913ed9


The commands and responses were tested against the versions listed above. Endpoint availability, payload schemas, permissions, and behavior may differ in other releases.


### Prerequisites


There are 4 prerequisites or considerations for this demonstration:


1. Your workstation or client must have access to the AWS CLI. Deploying the AWS CLI is beyond the scope of this article but can be completed using the[official AWS CLI documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) . The aws command should be available in your PATH, otherwise make a note of its location before continuing.
2. You must have either the Prism Central or AOS cluster’s extId/UUID. The` clustermgmt` v4 APIs can be used to get this. For example, to get the Prism Central cluster’s extId:` GET https://{{pc_ip}}:9440/api/clustermgmt/v4.4/config/clusters?$filter=config/clusterFunction/any(a:a eq Clustermgmt.Config.ClusterFunctionRef'PRISM_CENTRAL')`
3. ` cURL` , common in most environments today.
4. Optional:` jq` , for parsing and formatting JSON data.


## How do uploaded bundles work?


The Nutanix Objects Storage solution provides simple, secure, scale-out and AWS S3-compatible cloud object storage.


Built on almost the same foundation as Nutanix Objects Storage, Prism Central and LCM provide object storage via a service named Objects Lite. Objects Lite is an internal and ephemeral objects storage service made available to a number of different components, one of which is LCM bundles. It is not necessary to deploy or configure Objects Lite manually. For the purposes of this article, think of Objects Lite as temporary storage before the bundles are moved to the LCM catalog.


When uploading to objects storage locations, it is typical to deploy to a named bucket. LCM creates and manages its own Objects Lite bucket named **lcm-bundles** .


Once LCM bundles are uploaded to the` lcm-bundles` bucket, the Nutanix v4 lifecycle APIs (or SDKs) can be used to create a bundle for use with LCM. Whilst we’ll using the Nutanix v4 REST APIs today, the exact same process applies when using the Nutanix language-specific SDKs.


Let’s look at that process now.


## Scenario


Today’s simple scenario can be documented as follows:


- An I.T. administrator needs to automate the upload of LCM bundles from an automation VM
- The process must be monitored for success or failure
- The result must be logged for later analysis or reporting
- All steps must be scripted with no manual input after the bundles have been downloaded


- Administrator downloads bundles into` ~/nutanix/objects-lite` (path used in this demo)
- Uploads the bundles to the Objects Lite service managed by Prism Central
- Collects information about the uploaded bundle
- Creates an LCM-specific bundle for later deployment


## LCM Bundle Uploads


### Download bundle


If you would like to replicate the steps in this article, follow the steps below.


- From the[Nutanix Support Portal](https://portal.nutanix.com/) , navigate to Downloads


Nutanix Support Portal Downloads link


- Select Security within the Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure (NCI) section


Nutanix Support Portal Security link[Learn how to Secure your Hybrid Multi-Cloud in 30 mins: Part 1](https://www.nutanix.dev/learn-how-to-secure-your-hybrid-multi-cloud-in-30-mins-part-1/)


- Download the Security Dashboard CVE Data LCM Bundle


Download latest Security Dashboard CVE Data LCM Bundle


- Make a note of the file’s download location; this demo uses` ~/nutanix/objects-lite` .


### Generate base64-encoded Credentials


With the downloaded security CVE bundle now available, we can continue the next steps using the command line. If you prefer to generate base64-encoded credentials using an alternative method, ensure the encoded credentials are **not** suffixed with a newline character. Base64 encoding does not *encrypt* credentials.


These examples are illustrative only. Do not place production credentials in shell history, source files, screenshots, logs, or scripts. Use an approved secret-management method and follow your organization’s access-control and audit requirements.


To begin, open a terminal session and navigate to the folder containing the downloaded bundle.


#### Mac OS X, Linux and Windows PowerShell


```text
cd ~/nutanix/objects-lite
# printf ensures there's no newline character at the end of the base64-encoded string
printf '%s' '<username>:<password>' | base64
```


For example, if the username is` admin` and the password is` nutanix/4u` :


```text
cd ~/nutanix/objects-lite
printf '%s' 'admin:nutanix/4u' | base64
```


#### Windows Native PowerShell Only


```text
[Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('username:password'))
```


For example:


Using` printf` to generate a base64-encoded username and password (Mac OS X)


Using` printf` and native PowerShell to generate a base64-encoded username and password (Windows PowerShell)


All commands generate the base64-encoded username and password combination.


### Upload Bundle


For the remainder of this demo, we’ll use the following path:


```text
~/nutanix/objects-lite
```


Our demo environment’s Prism Central VM uses IP address **10.42.250.72** .


#### Configure AWS CLI Credentials


Select Option 1 or Option 2, depending on which method suits your requirements.


##### Option 1 – Credentials in script


Use the following commands to prepare AWS CLI for use with Objects Lite.


```text
# use the base64-encoded credentials for BOTH the access key and secret key
aws configure set aws_access_key_id <encoded credentials>
aws configure set aws_secret_access_key <encoded credentials>
aws configure set endpoint_url https://<pc-ip>:9440/api/prism/v4.0/objects/
```


For example, using the the base64-encoded credentials generated with username` admin` and password` nutanix/4u` :


```text
# use the base64-encoded credentials for BOTH the access key and secret key
aws configure set aws_access_key_id YWRtaW46bnV0YW5peC80dQ==
aws configure set aws_secret_access_key YWRtaW46bnV0YW5peC80dQ==
aws configure set endpoint_url https://10.42.250.72:9440/api/prism/v4.0/objects/
```


##### Option 2 –` credentials` file


Alternatively, a file named` ~/.aws/credentials` can be created and the credentials added directly to the file. The` aws configure` commands creates or modified this file regardless of the chosen method. If you prefer to create the file manually or deploy it using another method, the file is formatted as follows:


```text
[default]
aws_access_key_id = <encoded credentials>
aws_secret_access_key = <encoded credentials>
```


#### Upload Security CVE Bundle


With AWS CLI prepared, we can upload the bundle to Objects Lite:


```text
cd ~/nutanix/objects-lite
aws s3api put-object \
--bucket lcm-bundles \
--body ./lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1.tar.gz \
--key lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1 \
--no-verify-ssl
```


**Notes:**


- The` key` value is the filename without the extension;` lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1.tar.gz` becomes` lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1`
- ` --no-verify-ssl` disables SSL certificate verification and has been used here for demo purposes only. In a production environment, always use a certificate validation strategy consistent with your organisation’s security policies.


Uploading the LCM Security CVE bundle to Objects Lite; real credentials blurred


In the screenshot above, the response from a successful upload is the uploaded bundle’s expiration date and its Etag. The Etag is a critical requirement for the bundle creation step coming up, so note it down now:


```text
1d3a3cb3dd6a82ffd368b9913195f07f
```


#### Create LCM Bundle: Build Payload


So far we have:


- Uploaded the Security CVE bundle to Objects Lite
- Noted the uploaded bundle’s Etag


We can now build the payload for use with the Nutanix v4 LCM bundle creation request.


For example, the uploaded Security CVE bundle uploaded in this article would require the following payload:


```text
{
"name": "lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1",
"vendor": "NUTANIX",
"checksum": {
"hexDigest": "1d3a3cb3dd6a82ffd368b9913195f07f",
"$objectType": "lifecycle.v4.common.LcmMd5Sum"
},
"clusterExtId": "{{cluster_extid}}"
}
```


The method used to **send** the request may vary in production environments. This article is intended to provide a path towards integrating Objects Lite and Nutanix v4 APIs into a larger workflow, so we’ll use` cURL` here. The complete` cURL` command is as follows – note the use of single quotes within the double-quoted payload (` -d` within the command). This avoids the need to escape quoted values within the payload when using the command line.


One thing not covered yet is the` Ntnx-Request-Id` header. This header is mandatory for most Nutanix v4 API POST requests and ensures request[idempotence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotence) in the event the request is sent more than once.


```text
curl --insecure -X POST \
https://10.42.250.72:9440/api/lifecycle/v4.3/resources/bundles \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "Ntnx-Request-Id: e11126a2-cb59-44d6-9167-d7a79833528f" \
-H "Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46bnV0YW5peC80dQ==" \
-d '{ "name": "lcm_security_dashboard_cve_data_2026.10.1", "vendor": "NUTANIX", "checksum": { "hexDigest": "1d3a3cb3dd6a82ffd368b9913195f07f", "$objectType": "lifecycle.v4.common.LcmMd5Sum" }, "clusterExtId": "8f5d9aaf-9ef7-405e-93ff-77385d913ed9" }'
```


#### Create LCM Bundle: Send Request


Assuming there is a valid and working connection to the Prism Central IP address used in the` cURL` command, a successful request will respond with a JSON object. This JSON object contains information about the request, including a task reference` extId` :


```text
{
"data":{
"$reserved":{
"$fv":"v4.r2"
},
"$objectType":"prism.v4.config.TaskReference",
"extId":"ZXJnb24=:5e0a25a0-3358-5e38-bc8f-4dc3d7f0d878"
},
"$reserved":{
"$fv":"v4.r3"
},
"$objectType":"lifecycle.v4.resources.CreateBundleApiResponse"
}
```


Many of the Nutanix v4 APIs and SDKs will return a JSON response similar to this example. The common format shown here, including the associated task` extId` , allows a scripting administrator to quickly integrate most Nutanix v4 API requests into custom monitoring workflows.


#### Create LCM Bundle: Check Response


With the task` extId` available, we can use the Nutanix v4` prism` APIs to analyse the LCM create bundle request.


We know the task’s` extId` is` ZXJnb24=:5e0a25a0-3358-5e38-bc8f-4dc3d7f0d878` and can now send a` prism` namespace request as follows. This example uses` jq` to get the task result ONLY, omitting all other fields. This is optional and may not suit all environments.


```text
curl --silent --insecure -X GET \
https://10.42.250.72:9440/api/prism/v4.4/config/tasks/ZXJnb24=:5e0a25a0-3358-5e38-bc8f-4dc3d7f0d878 \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46bnV0YW5peC80dQ==" | jq '.data.status'
```


This screenshot shows the task as **SUCCEEDED.** The uploaded bundle is now available for deployment using Nutanix Lifecycle Manager.


SUCCEEDED status after sending a` prism` GET task request


### Create LCM Bundle: Integration


After walking through this process, let’s summarise the complete workflow.


1. Download bundles into` ~/nutanix/objects-lite`
2. Use the AWS CLI to upload bundles into Objects Lite on Prism Central
3. Use the Nutanix v4` lifecycle` APIs to create an LCM bundle
4. Use the Nutanix v4` prism` APIs to analyse the result, checking for success or failure


In this example, the upload, registration, and task-status checks are performed programmatically after the bundle is downloaded.


## Next Steps


Now that the LCM bundle has been created, what next? In a production environment, next steps could be as follows. These steps are beyond the scope of this specific article.


- Run an LCM inventory
- Use the Nutanix v4` lifecycle` APIs to query which clusters need the update in question
- Build target payloads for the target clusters
- Use the Nutanix v4` lifecycle` APIs to apply the updates
- Use the Nutanix v4` prism` APIs to monitor update progress and report on the results


## Wrapping Up


In today’s article, we’ve seen how the Nutanix v4 APIs can be used in conjunction with the AWS CLI to upload and prepare Nutanix Lifecycle Manager updates. This approach allows automation of a complete, end-to-end update process, minimising the amount of manual interaction required.


For more information, see[Nutanix Lifecycle Manager](https://www.nutanix.com/products/life-cycle-manager) . Thanks for reading.
